title: Hobbes’s twist on the Ship of Theseus leaves you with two rival ships
body: The Greek biographer Plutarch tells how the Athenians preserved the thirty-oared ship of the mythical king Theseus, taking out the old planks as they decayed and putting in new, strong timber, until philosophers argued over whether it was still the same ship. In *De Corpore* (1655) Thomas Hobbes added a twist: suppose someone kept every old plank and put them back together in the same order. Now two ships have a claim to be the original, one with the same **form** and one with the same **matter**. The puzzle is about identity over time: what makes anything, including a person, the same thing when its parts change?

slides.alt: Animation of a Greek galley in profile on blue sea. One by one its 38 weathered hull planks are swapped for fresh honey-coloured wood, and the old ones pile up on a stone quay. Then they fly back together into a second ship, labelled matter, while the repaired one is labelled form.
slides.music: “Ascending the Vale” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Replace all 38 planks, then rebuild a second ship from the old ones. Which one is the ship of Theseus?
slides.takeaway: The repaired ship keeps the form, the rebuilt one the matter: two good answers to one question. Plutarch told of the repairs; Hobbes added the ship rebuilt from the old planks.

slides.text: They took away the old planks as they decayed, putting in new and strong timber in their places, insomuch that this ship became a standing example among the philosophers, for the logical question of things that grow.

slides.heading: Two ways to be the same ship

left.label: Form
left.text: The repaired ship keeps the original’s form through a complete change of material: every plank is new.

right.label: Matter
right.text: The rebuilt ship is made of the original planks, put back together in the same order.

slides.heading: Match each to its part in the puzzle
slides.explanation: Plutarch reports the repairs; Hobbes imagined a second ship of old planks; Lewis treated objects as time slices; Ise is rebuilt every 20 years.

slides.question: Japan’s Ise Shrine is rebuilt with fresh timber on a fixed cycle. How many years?
slides.explanation: The shrine is rebuilt every 20 years, yet treated as the same sacred place: a living version of the ship of Theseus puzzle.

slides.heading: Real ships of Theseus
slides.text: Only a small part of the frigate USS *Constitution*, launched in 1797, is thought to be original wood. The submersible *Alvin* is taken apart every few years, and every one of its components has been replaced at least once.

slides.heading: Why it matters
slides.text: In the philosophy of mind, the puzzle has inspired many proposed answers to what keeps a person the same person over time.
